explain.say: It starts when something irritates the lining inside your nose, such as dust, pollen or a cold virus. A nerve called the trigeminal nerve carries the alarm to a sneeze centre in the brainstem.

faq.a: Sneezing is a reflex that clears irritants such as dust, pollen or germs out of the nose. A powerful burst of air carries them away so they do not go deeper into your airways.

faq.q: What makes your nose tickle before a sneeze?
faq.a: Nerve endings in the nose lining detect irritants. They send signals along the trigeminal nerve to the brainstem, which you feel as a tickle and which can trigger the sneeze reflex.
asks: Tell me about the tickle in the nose

faq.q: How fast does a sneeze come out?
faq.a: Measurements vary, but sneezes have been recorded at around 10 to 20 metres per second at the start, and the droplets can travel several metres.
asks: Tell me about the blast out
How far does a sneeze go?

faq.q: Why do we shut our eyes when we sneeze?
faq.a: Closing the eyes is part of the reflex wiring: the same brainstem pathway that runs the sneeze also makes the eyelids close. It is automatic, not because your eyes could pop out, which is a myth.
asks: Can you sneeze with your eyes open?

faq.q: Why do some people sneeze in bright light?
faq.a: About one in four or five people have a photic sneeze reflex. Scientists think the nerve signals from the eyes and nose are close together in the brain, so a sudden bright light can trigger a sneeze.
asks: Why does sunlight make me sneeze?

facts: The sneeze reflex is coordinated by a centre in the brainstem.
The photic sneeze reflex, sneezing in bright light, affects roughly 18 to 35 percent of people.

quiz.say: Which part of the body runs the sneeze reflex?
quiz.show: Which part of the body runs the sneeze reflex?
quiz.why: A sneeze centre in the brainstem coordinates the breath, the throat closing and the blast.
